messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 57
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Latin American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Physical Therapist
  trauma_type: Natural disaster
  pcl5: 39

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Somatic (Nausea): Feeling nauseous, Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Visual (Water/Flooding): Water, flooding, or large bodies of water
  Maladaptive Strategies: Dissociate Deliberately: deliberately try to leave my body or blank out, Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Going Out: Going out
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Safe Zone Only: I only feel safe in a very limited number of places, Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds
  Memory: Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory, Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Memory
  - Memory → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Memory → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Triggers

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Marisol Alvarez is a 57-year-old physical therapist who has lived for years in a low-lying coastal part of the United States, and she still dates her life as before and after the hurricane. During the storm, she had stayed in her house longer than she now thinks was wise, trying to bring photo albums and medications upstairs while rain came in under the doors and the street outside turned into a fast-moving brown current. What stays with her most is not a single clean picture but the sense of rising water and the sick, rolling nausea that overtook her as she stood in it, hearing neighbors shout names through the wind and darkness. By the time she was evacuated by boat, she remembers clutching the side and feeling she had crossed into something unreal. When she tries to describe it now, she often says it feels as if it happened to someone else, and yet when it comes back, it brings a crushing grief for her home, her neighborhood, and the person she believes she was before that night.

In the months afterward, Marisol found that the event did not return as a straightforward memory. More often she would be seized by the same emotional force without any clear image at all: a sudden wave of dread and sorrow in her body, accompanied by nausea, as if the storm were happening again somewhere just outside awareness. At other times, a very specific cue would pull the memory forward. Passing a flooded underpass, seeing standing water after hard rain, or even looking too long at a wide expanse of water could make her stomach turn before she fully understood why. Hearing storm names on the news during hurricane season or hearing a patient mention the name of the neighborhood she lost could do the same. Those moments seemed to unlock the memory, even when all she could grasp was the feeling of catastrophe and grief rather than a full scene.

Her work has made this particularly difficult. As a physical therapist, she moves through a busy rehabilitation clinic where there are therapy pools in the larger medical complex and where patients often arrive wet on rainy days, shaking out umbrellas by the entrance. She has become acutely alert to unexpected sounds there—the slam of a heavy door, a crash from dropped equipment, the overhead weather alert on someone’s phone—and once she is keyed up, she scans for signs of water, certain names, or anything that might set her off. On days when she has slept badly, which is most nights, this vigilance is worse. She describes feeling safe only at home and in one exam room at work with no windows; beyond those places, she is braced for something to break through. In that state, even minor cues can become potent, so that nausea, a glimpse of pooling rain in the parking lot, or hearing a familiar storm-related name can rapidly pull her back into the emotional memory of the hurricane.

What she does then is to try not to be there at all. When the feeling surges, Marisol deliberately goes blank. She fixes her gaze, lets her mind float away, and tries to leave her body until the moment passes. At home she spends long stretches dwelling on who she was before the hurricane—someone she remembers as freer, more spontaneous, willing to drive anywhere, willing to be near the ocean. These habits have narrowed her life. She declines invitations, avoids going out unless she has to, and keeps to a small circuit of places she has judged safe. Yet the more she blanks out when the grief rises, the less the memory feels like her own when it returns, as though it remains unprocessed and foreign. The more she lives in comparisons with her former self, the more sharply the loss is felt whenever the memory is touched.

Over time this has tightened into a pattern she can now see but has not been able to interrupt. Because she avoids going out, ordinary exposure to the world has become rarer and more charged; a necessary trip in heavy rain, a water feature outside the hospital, or a stray name overheard in a waiting room can hit with disproportionate force. When triggers break through, they bring the familiar nausea and the same engulfing grief, often without pictures. That in turn makes her want to disappear inward again, to detach, to get home, to stop moving through places where anything might remind her. Her sleep has worsened, and she arrives at work already tense, listening for sudden sounds and trying to keep her day confined to the safest corners of the clinic.

Marisol finally sought help after leaving work abruptly during a summer storm warning, shaken by a combination of thunder, standing water in the parking lot, and a patient mentioning a flooded street with the same name as her old block. She sat in her car, nauseated and tearful, unable to explain to a colleague why she could not go back inside. What frightens her most is that her world has become so small and that the memory still feels both distant and overpowering, as if it can seize her body without ever becoming fully knowable. What she hopes for, cautiously, is to feel present in her own life again and not be ruled by water, names, and the fear of what they will stir up.
